query: For high-entropy alloys intended for extreme environments, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties? State the intervention without limiting its class, the proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the temperature and application boundaries under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose outcome would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small trace of boron (~0.1 at.%) during alloy synthesis and employing a controlled cooling treatment will trigger the precipitation of fine boride phases along the grain boundaries and promote a serrated boundary morphology. This intervention is expected to strengthen grain-boundary cohesion and reduce local strain concentration at elevated temperature, thereby significantly enhancing tensile ductility and creep resistance in refractory high‐entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy) processed without intentional boron doping, featuring predominantly straight grain boundaries and relying on solid-solution plus conventional precipitation strengthening.
generation.intervention: Introduce ~0.1 at.% boron during synthesis (or via minor alloying addition) followed by a controlled cooling heat treatment designed to enable boride precipitation at grain boundaries and the development of serrated grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Performance is to be evaluated under elevated temperature conditions around 650°C, where intergranular decohesion is known to compromise ductility and creep resistance.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, coherent intergranular boride precipitates that both pin and undulate the grain boundaries (i.e. induce serration).
generation.mechanism: The boride precipitates enhance grain-boundary cohesion and act as local stress distributors, reducing the tendency for intergranular crack initiation and propagation. The resulting serrated grain boundary morphology delocalizes strain during high-temperature deformation, thereby impeding the motion of dislocations at the boundaries and retarding creep deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy without boron, the boron-doped alloy should exhibit a markedly increased tensile ductility (for example, fracture strain improved by a factor of approximately 3–3.5) at 650°C and a substantial reduction (potentially 3–4 times lower) in the minimum creep strain rate, leading to an extended creep rupture life.
generation.baseline: The same refractory high-entropy alloy composition processed without boron addition and with predominantly straight grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: This enhancement is predicted to be effective in high-temperature regimes around 650°C, as encountered in extreme service conditions (e.g., in nuclear reactor environments), but the effect may vary outside this temperature window.
generation.uncertainty: While studies (PMC9572892 and PMC9848264) support boron-induced intergranular precipitation and serrated boundaries improving ductility and creep performance, the quantitative impact on tensile yield strength and the detailed role of the induced edge-dislocation dynamics at 650°C remain to be determined. The extrapolation from compressive and room-temperature data to elevated-temperature tensile behavior introduces uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of refractory high-entropy alloy samples with identical base compositions. One group is doped with ~0.1 at.% boron and subjected to a controlled cooling heat treatment aimed at producing intergranular boride precipitation and serrated boundaries; the control group is processed identically without boron. Conduct high-temperature tensile tests and creep experiments at 650°C, complemented by microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM) to verify the formation of boride precipitates and serrated grain boundaries.
measurements: Tensile fracture strain and yield strength at 650°C
Minimum creep strain rate and overall creep rupture life at 650°C
Grain boundary morphology parameters (e.g., serration wavelength and amplitude) via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not display statistically significant improvements (e.g., less than a ~3× increase in fracture strain or a less than 3–4× reduction in creep rate) compared to the control, or if no clear difference in grain boundary morphology is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion, the work hardenability and ductility were effectively improved with the addition of boron.Keywords: refractory alloy, high-entropy alloy, boride, grain boundary, mechanical prop

ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
